bug_class: SQL injection (write-then-read-back / second-order style) → PII + resume-token disclosure
title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in a public quote flow ($4,000)
root_cause: A JSON field on a public "retrieve" endpoint was concatenated into a SQL string literal; the endpoint had zero auth (its own API spec said so); one shared backend table served several front ends, so the blast radius covered the whole quote system.
discovery_method: Posted a JSON body to the public retrieve endpoint, injected into the field to stage a quote under a reference he controlled, then fetched that reference back — the field returned already evaluated by the DB, exposing selected columns (names, emails, phones, addresses, resume tokens).
takeaway: His tip: in any "come back to your saved thing later" flow, go straight for lookup fields; if one field writes and another reads it back, treat it as an oracle. Read API specs for endpoints marked unauthenticated.
payload: POST JSON to the public /retrieve endpoint; inject into the reflected field; stage a record under a controlled reference; GET the reference back to read DB-evaluated columns (second-order / write-then-read-back)

bug_class: Auth bypass via path normalisation mismatch
title: /./ path normalisation past a login wall into an admin console
root_cause: The login check matched the exact raw path, but the router normalised the path afterwards, so /admin/./ failed the exact match yet still routed to /admin.
discovery_method: Testing path variants (/./, //, %2e, trailing slash) against protected prefixes.
takeaway: Whenever auth middleware and router parse paths differently, try dot-segments and encodings; check every layer (proxy, middleware, framework router).
payload: Append /./ (also //, trailing dots, %2e) to a 403/login-gated path: /admin/./ passes the exact-match auth check then normalises to /admin at the router

bug_class: Auth bypass / broken JWT-style token validation
title: $8,000 auth bypass on HackerOne — token signature not verified
root_cause: The server accepted tokens without verifying their signature, so a forged/modified token was trusted.
discovery_method: Tampering with token claims and signatures (strip, alter, re-sign with none/self key) and checking whether the server still accepts them.
takeaway: Always test whether signatures are actually verified, not just parsed.
payload: Tamper JWT/token claims and signature (strip, alter, alg=none, self-sign) and confirm the server still accepts it

title: $1,200 Bugcrowd dependency confusion
root_cause: An internal package name used by the target was unclaimed on the public registry, so a public package with that name could be pulled by builds.
discovery_method: Harvesting package names (JS bundles, manifests, errors) and checking them against the public registry.
takeaway: Claim-check every internal package name you find; report with a benign callback-only PoC per program rules.
payload: Harvest internal package names from JS bundles/manifests; publish/claim a benign package of the same name on the public registry; confirm resolution with a callback-only PoC

title: XSS-challenge solution thread (10 parts)
root_cause: The page parsed the query twice with different logic; a regex char class `[?|&]` (pipe treated literally) let a crafted parameter be picked up by one parser but not the other.
discovery_method: Reading the client-side parameter extraction code.
takeaway: Look for differential parsing of the same URL; regex char-class mistakes are common.
payload: Send two query params: ?|targetUrl=<validated> and &targetUrl=javascript:... — one extraction validates, the other reaches location.href (regex [?|&] treats | literally)

bug_class: OAuth redirect_uri validation → token theft / ATO
title: iOS OAuth client accepts any protocol in redirect_uri
root_cause: The iPhone app's OAuth client (a client_id different from the web app's) allowed any protocol in redirect_uri because iOS deep links use custom schemes; a malicious app could start the flow in Safari with the callback pointing at itself and receive the user's credentials.
discovery_method: Noticed an unfamiliar client_id in the OAuth flow, traced it to the iOS app, then tested redirect_uri protocols.
takeaway: Enumerate every client_id (web, iOS, Android, desktop) and test redirect_uri validation separately for each.
payload: Register a malicious iOS app for the custom URL scheme accepted as OAuth redirect_uri; start the flow in Safari with callback pointing at the malicious app to capture the code/token

bug_class: Smart contract: unsafe callback + stale approval + EIP-7702
title: EtherFi helper contract hack — three holes lined up
root_cause: AtomicQueue called a callback on a user-provided address and treated a successful call as intent (no required return data); the victim had a year-old hanging approval; EIP-7702 delegation made the victim EOA execute code, so the callback no longer simply failed.
discovery_method: Post-incident analysis.
takeaway: Require specific callback return data; revoke stale approvals; re-audit EOA-assumptions after EIP-7702.
payload: Chain: unchecked callback return in AtomicQueue + victim stale approval + EIP-7702 delegation so the EOA executes attacker code on callback

title: Solana governance: any validator could silently erase its delegators' dissenting votes
root_cause: For its first 6 weeks on mainnet the governance program let a validator erase delegators' dissenting votes; without the fix SGP-0002 would have failed by 0.02 percentage points (per post).
discovery_method: Found with their tool Crucible (per post).
takeaway: Governance vote-accounting is security-critical; check who can overwrite or reset another party's vote record.

bug_class: L2 node / bridge logic (DoS, asset-migration blocking)
title: Polygon zkEVM: reverted non-free claim txs mark deposit counts and block L1→L2 claims (Immunefi)
root_cause: Claim txs were free (gas price 0) and pre-executed before entering the pool; only free+reverted claims were rejected. A claim with non-zero gas that reverted fell into the else-branch, was added to the pool and marked its deposit count as used — so attackers could DoS sequencer/prover cheaply and pre-burn any deposit count so the legitimate claim was rejected.
discovery_method: Reading the node's special-case handling of claim-tx pre-execution results and enumerating every branch (free/non-free × revert/non-revert).
takeaway: Special-case fee logic in rollup nodes is fertile ground; enumerate all branch combinations. Fixed by removing the special gas logic; Immunefi added a new impact category after the report.
payload: Submit a non-free (gas>0) claim tx that reverts: it falls into the else branch, is pooled and marks its deposit count used, blocking the legitimate L1->L2 claim and DoSing the sequencer
